arXiv:1103.1292v1 [math.AP] 07 Mar 2011

The Cauchy problem for the DMKP equation

Amin Esfahani Note: Address: School of Mathematics and Computer Science, Damghan University, Damghan, Postal Code 36716-41167, Iran.  E-mail: amin@impa.br, esfahani@du.ac.ir
Abstract

In this work, we study the dissipation-modified Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation in two space-dimensional case. We establish that the Cauchy problem for this equation is locally well-posed in anisotropic Sobolev spaces. We show in some sense that our result is sharp. We also prove the global well-posedness for this equation under suitable conditions.

Keywords: DMKP equation, Well-posedness, Anisotropic Sobolev spaces.
Mathematical subject classification: 35B30, 35Q55, 35Q72.

1 Introduction

In this work, we consider the initial value problem for the dissipation-modified Kadomtsev-Petviashvili (DMKP) equation

{(ut+ux​x​x+uux+α(ux​x+ux​x​x​x)+β(u2)x​x)x+εuy​y=0,(x,y)∈ℝ2,t≥0,u⁡(x,y,0)=φ⁡(x,y),\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}{\left(u_{t}+u_{xxx}+uu_{x}+\alpha(u_{xx}+u_{xxxx})+\beta(u^{2})_{xx}\right)}_{x}+\varepsilon u_{yy}=0,\qquad(x,y)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2},\,\,t\geq 0,\\ \\ u(x,y,0)=\varphi(x,y),\end{array}\right. (1.1)

where α>0\alpha>0 and β\beta are real constants and ε=±1\varepsilon=\pm 1. The DMKP equation (1.1) arises in studying spontaneous generation of long waves in the presence of a conservation law in isotropic systems (e.g., Bénard-Marangoni waves), near the instability threshold [1, 8, 18]. In [6, 7], the author has also investigated another version of (1.1).

Equation (1.1) is also a natural two-dimensional version of the KdV-Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KdV-KS) equation

ut+ux​x​x+u​ux+α⁡(ux​x+ux​x​x​x)=0,u_{t}+u_{xxx}+uu_{x}+\alpha(u_{xx}+u_{xxxx})=0, (1.2)

which arises in interesting physical situations, for example as a model for long waves on a viscous fluid flowing down an inclined plane [20] and to derive drift waves in a plasma [5].

The DMKP equation, when β=0\beta=0, is a dissipative version of the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili (KP) equation

(ut+ux​x​x+u​ux)x+ε​uy​y=0,(u_{t}+u_{xxx}+uu_{x})_{x}+\varepsilon u_{yy}=0, (1.3)

which is universal model for nearly one directional weakly nonlinear dispersive waves with weak transverse effects. The KP equation, in turn, is a two-dimensional extension of the KdV equation

ut+ux​x​x+u​ux=0.u_{t}+u_{xxx}+uu_{x}=0. (1.4)

Our principal aim here is to study the local well-posedness for the initial value problem associated to the DMKP equation in the anisotropic Sobolev spaces Hs1,s2​(ℝ2)H^{s_{1},s_{2}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), s1,s2∈ℝs_{1},s_{2}\in{\mathbb{R}}.

In the past decades, Bourgain developed a new method, clarified by Ginibre in [9], for the study of the Cauchy problem for nonlinear dispersive equations. This method was further successfully applied to Schrödinger, KdV and KPII equations (cf. [2, 3, 4, 11, 12]). The original Bourgain method makes extensive use of the Strichartz inequalities in order to derive the bilinear estimates corresponding to the nonlinearity. On the other hand, Kenig et al. [11, 12] simplified Bourgain’s proof and improved the bilinear estimates using only elementary techniques, such as Cauchy-Schwartz inequality and simple calculus inequalities (see also [10, 19]).

It was also shown by Molinet and Ribaud [14, 15, 16] that the Bourgain spaces can be used to study the Cauchy problems associated to semi-linear equations with a linear part containing both dispersive and dissipative terms; and consequently this applies to the KdV-Burgers (KdVB) equation

ut+ux​x​x+u​ux=ux​xu_{t}+u_{xxx}+uu_{x}=u_{xx} (1.5)

and the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili-Burgers (KPB) equation

(ut+ux​x​x+u​ux−ux​x)x+ε​uy​y=0.(u_{t}+u_{xxx}+uu_{x}-u_{xx})_{x}+\varepsilon u_{yy}=0. (1.6)

By introducing a Bourgain space associated to the usual KP equation, related only to the dispersive part of the linear symbol of (1.6), Molinet and Ribaud [15] proved global existence for the Cauchy problem associated to the KPB equation (1.6), by using Strichartz-type estimates for the KP equation injected into the framework of Bourgain spaces. More precisely, authors in [15] showed the KPB-I equation (ε=−1\varepsilon=-1) is locally well-posed in Hs1,s2​(ℝ2)H^{s_{1},s_{2}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) if s1>0s_{1}>0 and s2≥0s_{2}\geq 0; and the KPB-II equation (ε=1\varepsilon=1) is locally well-posed in Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) if s≥0s\geq 0. The global well-posedness followed by means of a priori estimates.

Recently Kojok in [13] obtained a sharp result by proving that the KPB-II equation is globally well-posed in Hs1,s2​(ℝ2)H^{s_{1},s_{2}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) for s1>−1/2s_{1}>-1/2 and s2≥0s_{2}\geq 0.

In this paper, we will apply the ideas of [14, 15, 16] and introduce a Bourgain-type space associated to the KP equation. This space is in fact the intersection of the space introduced in [4] and of a Sobolev space. The advantage of this space is that it contains both the dissipative and dispersive parts of the linear symbol of (1.1). Next we establish the local existence for (1.1) with initial value φ∈Hs1,s2​(ℝ2)\varphi\in H^{s_{1},s_{2}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) when s1>−1/2s_{1}>-1/2 and s2≥0s_{2}\geq 0; and we also show that the Cauchy problem (1.1) is globally well-posed in φ∈Hs1,s2​(ℝ2)\varphi\in H^{s_{1},s_{2}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) if β=0\beta=0, s1>−1s_{1}>-1 and s2≥0s_{2}\geq 0. We prove also that our local existence theorem is optimal by constructing a counterexample showing that the application φ→u\varphi\to u from Hs1,s2​(ℝ2)H^{s_{1},s_{2}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) to C⁡([0,T],Hs1,s2​(ℝ2))C([0,T];H^{s_{1},s_{2}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})) cannot be regular for s1<−1/2s_{1}<-1/2 and s2=0s_{2}=0.

This existence result, in some sense, is quite surprising. There is no difference in the existence result for ε=±1\varepsilon=\pm 1 in (1.1). However, despising the dissipation terms in (1.1), we obtain the KP equation (1.3), where the KP-I and KP-II models are quite distinct.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce some notations and our main results. In Section 3, we derive linear estimates and some smoothing properties for the operator arising from (1.1) in the Bourgain spaces (Lemma 3.2). Section 4 is devoted to establish bilinear estimates by using Strichartz-type estimates for the KP equation. In Section 5, using bilinear estimates, a standard fixed point argument and some smoothing properties, we prove uniqueness and local existence of the solution of (1.1) in anisotropic Sobolev space Hs1,s2​(ℝ2)H^{s_{1},s_{2}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) with s1>−1/2s_{1}>-1/2 and s2≥0s_{2}\geq 0; and global existence of the solution of (1.1), with β=0\beta=0, in Hs1,s2​(ℝ2)H^{s_{1},s_{2}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) with s1>−1s_{1}>-1 and s2≥0s_{2}\geq 0. Finally in Section 6 we show that our results are sharp in the sense that the flow map of the DMKP equation fail to be C2C^{2} in Hs1,0​(ℝ2)H^{s_{1},0}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})) for s1<−1/2s_{1}<-1/2.

2 Notations and Main Results

Hs1,s2={f∈𝒮′(ℝ2);∥f∥Hs1,s2=∥⟨ξ⟩s1⟨η⟩s2f^(ξ,η)∥Lξ,η2<∞}.\displaystyle H^{s_{1},s_{2}}=\left\{f\in\mathscr{S}^{\prime}({\mathbb{R}}^{2});\;\|f\|_{H^{s_{1},s_{2}}}=\|\langle\xi\rangle^{s_{1}}\langle\eta\rangle^{s_{2}}\widehat{f}(\xi,\eta)\|_{L^{2}_{\xi,\eta}}<\infty\right\}.

U⁡(t)=exp⁡(i​t​P​(Dx,Dy)),U(t)=\exp({\rm i}tP(D_{x},D_{y})),

where P⁡(Dx,Dy)P(D_{x},D_{y}) is the Fourier multiplier with symbol P⁡(ζ)=P⁡(ξ,η)=ξ3−ε​η2/ξP(\zeta)=P(\xi,\eta)=\xi^{3}-\varepsilon\eta^{2}/\xi, with ε=±1\varepsilon=\pm 1.

We introduce a Bourgain space which is in relation with both the dissipative and dispersive parts of (1.1) at the same time, we define this space by

Xb,s1,s2={f∈𝒮′​(ℝ3):‖f‖Xb,s1,s2<∞},X^{b,s_{1},s_{2}}=\left\{f\in\mathscr{S}^{\prime}({\mathbb{R}}^{3})\;:\;\|f\|_{X^{b,s_{1},s_{2}}}<\infty\right\},

equipped with the norm

‖f‖Xb,s1,s2=‖⟨i​σ+ϱ⁡(ξ)⟩b​⟨ξ⟩s1​⟨η⟩s2​f^​(τ,ζ)‖L2​(ℝ3),\|f\|_{X^{b,s_{1},s_{2}}}=\left\|\langle{\rm i}\sigma+\varrho(\xi)\rangle^{b}\langle\xi\rangle^{s_{1}}\langle\eta\rangle^{s_{2}}\widehat{f}(\tau,\zeta)\right\|_{L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{3})},

where σ=τ−P⁡(ζ)\sigma=\tau-P(\zeta) and ϱ⁡(ξ)=ξ4−ξ2\varrho(\xi)=\xi^{4}-\xi^{2}.

‖f‖Xb,s1,s2≈‖U⁡(−t)​f‖Htb​Hx,ys1,s2+‖f‖Lt2​Hx,ys1+2​b,s2.\|f\|_{X^{b,s_{1},s_{2}}}\approx\|U(-t)f\|_{H^{b}_{t}H^{s_{1},s_{2}}_{x,y}}+\|f\|_{L_{t}^{2}H^{s_{1}+2b,s_{2}}_{x,y}}.

By the Duhamel integral formulation, equation (1.1) can be written

u⁡(t)=W⁡(t)​φ−∫0tW⁡(t−t′)​Λ​(u2​(t′))​d​t′,t≥0,u(t)=W(t)\varphi-\int_{0}^{t}W(t-t^{\prime})\Lambda(u^{2}(t^{\prime})){\rm d}t^{\prime},\qquad t\geq 0, (2.1)

To prove the local existence result, we will apply a fixed point argument to a truncated version of (2.1) which is defined on all the real axis by

u⁡(t)=θ⁡(t)​W​(t)​φ−θ⁡(t)​χℝ+​(t)​∫0tW⁡(t−t′)​Λ​(θT2​(t′)​u2​(t′))​d​t′,t≥0,u(t)=\theta(t)W(t)\varphi-\theta(t)\chi_{{\mathbb{R}}^{+}}(t)\int_{0}^{t}W(t-t^{\prime})\Lambda\left(\theta_{T}^{2}(t^{\prime})u^{2}(t^{\prime})\right){\rm d}t^{\prime},\qquad t\geq 0, (2.2)

where t∈ℝt\in{\mathbb{R}} and θ\theta indicates a time cutoff function:

θ∈C0∞(ℝ),supp(θ)⊂[−2,2],θ≡1on[−1,1],\theta\in C_{0}^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}),\quad{\rm supp}(\theta)\subset[-2,2],\quad\theta\equiv 1\quad\mbox{on}\,\;[-1,1],

and θT(⋅)=θ(⋅/T)\theta_{T}(\cdot)=\theta(\cdot/T).

We note that that if uu solves (2.2) then uu is a solution of (2.1) on [0,T][0,T], T≤1T\leq 1. Thus it is sufficient to solve (2.2) for a small time (T≤1T\leq 1 is enough).

Let us now state our results.

THEOREM 2.1

Let s1>−1/2s_{1}>-1/2, s2≥0s_{2}\geq 0, s1′∈(−1/2,min{0,s1}]s^{\prime}_{1}\in(-1/2,\min\{0,s_{1}\}] and φ∈Hs1,s2\varphi\in H^{s_{1},s_{2}}. Then there exist a time T=T⁡(‖φ‖Hs1′,0)>0T=T(\|\varphi\|_{H^{s^{\prime}_{1},0}})>0 and a unique solution uu of (1.1) in

𝒴T=C⁡([0,T],Hs1,s2)∩XT1/2,s1,s2.\mathscr{Y}_{T}=C([0,T],H^{s_{1},s_{2}})\cap X_{T}^{1/2,s_{1},s_{2}}. (2.3)

Moreover, uu belongs C⁡([0,T],Hs1,s2)∩C⁡((0,T],H∞,s2)C([0,T];H^{s_{1},s_{2}})\cap C((0,T];H^{\infty,s_{2}}) and the map φ↦u\varphi\mapsto u is analytic from Hs1,s2H^{s_{1},s_{2}} to 𝒴T\mathscr{Y}_{T}.

THEOREM 2.2

Let s<−1/2s<-1/2. Then it does not exist a time T>0T>0 such that equation (1.1) admits a unique solution in C⁡([0,T),Hs,0)C([0,T);H^{s,0}) for any initial data in some ball of Hs,0H^{s,0} centered at the origin and such that the map φ→u\varphi\to u is C2C^{2}-differentiable at the origin from Hs,0H^{s,0} to C⁡([0,T],Hs,0)C([0,T],H^{s,0}).

THEOREM 2.3

Let β=0\beta=0. Then Theorem 2.1 holds for s1>−1s_{1}>-1, s2≥0s_{2}\geq 0 and φ∈Hs1,s2\varphi\in H^{s_{1},s_{2}}; and the corresponding local solution uu of the Cauchy problem (1.1) extends globally in time.

LEMMA 3.2

Let 0<δ≤1/20<\delta\leq 1/2 and s1,s2∈ℝs_{1},s_{2}\in{\mathbb{R}}, there exists C=Cδ>0C=C_{\delta}>0 such that for all w∈X−1/2+δ,s1−4δ,s2w\in X^{-1/2+\delta,s_{1}-4\delta,s_{2}}, we have

‖θ(t)χℝ+(t)∫0tW(t−t′)w(t′)dt′‖X1/2,s1,s2≤C∥w∥X−1/2+δ,s1−4δ,s2.\left\|\theta(t)\chi_{{\mathbb{R}}^{+}}(t)\int_{0}^{t}W(t-t^{\prime})w(t^{\prime}){\rm d}t^{\prime}\right\|_{X^{1/2,s_{1},s_{2}}}\leq C\|w\|_{X^{-1/2+\delta,s_{1}-4\delta,s_{2}}}. (3.6)

Proof. Let b∈ℝb\in{\mathbb{R}}. For ζ∈ℝ2\zeta\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2} fixed, we define the following time-Sobolev space

𝒴ζb={w∈𝒮′(ℝ3);∥w∥𝒴ζb=∥⟨iτ+ϱ(ξ)⟩bw^(τ,ζ)∥Lτ2<∞}.\mathscr{Y}_{\zeta}^{b}=\{w\in\mathscr{S}^{\prime}({\mathbb{R}}^{3});\;\|w\|_{\mathscr{Y}_{\zeta}^{b}}=\|\langle{\rm i}\tau+\varrho(\xi)\rangle^{b}\widehat{w}(\tau,\zeta)\|_{L_{\tau}^{2}}<\infty\}.

First we shall show that for ζ∈ℝ2\zeta\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}, 0<δ≤1/20<\delta\leq 1/2 and w∈𝒮⁡(ℝ3)w\in\mathscr{S}({\mathbb{R}}^{3}), the following estimate holds:

Let s1,s2∈ℝs_{1},s_{2}\in{\mathbb{R}} and 0<δ≤1/20<\delta\leq 1/2. Then for all f∈X−1/2+δ,s1−4δ,s2f\in X^{-1/2+\delta,s_{1}-4\delta,s_{2}}, we have

|∫kζet​ϱ​(ξ)​𝒦​(ζ,ζ1,t)​d​ζ1|≳|kζ|​N−4−ϵ≳N−1−ϵ.\left|\int_{k_{\zeta}}{\rm e}^{t\varrho(\xi)}\mathscr{K}(\zeta,\zeta_{1},t){\rm d}\zeta_{1}\right|\gtrsim|k_{\zeta}|N^{-4-\epsilon}\gtrsim N^{-1-\epsilon}.

Therefore it follows from (6.2) that

1≳‖u2,N‖Hs,02≳N−4​s−6​N−2−2​ϵ​∫3​N/23​N∫−4​N29​N2(|ξ|+ξ2)2​(1+ξ2)s​𝑑ζ≳N−2​s−1−2​ϵ.1\gtrsim\|u_{2,N}\|_{H^{s,0}}^{2}\gtrsim N^{-4s-6}N^{-2-2\epsilon}\int_{3N/2}^{3N}\int_{-4N^{2}}^{9N^{2}}(|\xi|+\xi^{2})^{2}(1+\xi^{2})^{s}{\rm d}\zeta\gtrsim N^{-2s-1-2\epsilon}.

This leads to a contradiction for N≫1N\gg 1, since we have s<−1/2−2ϵs<-1/2-2\epsilon; and the proof of Theorem 2.2 is complete. □\square
